Thanks for the call earlier — the summary was super helpful. A couple of follow-ups from my side as we scope Dedicated: 

- Latency target: P95 <= 200ms for single-turn customer prompts (avg prompt length ~120 tokens).
- Streaming: we need chunked streaming for progressive output to our front-end (websocket).
- Concurrency: plan for ~150 concurrent active sessions at peak; spikes to 300 for flash sales events.
- Throughput: expect ~10k tokens/sec aggregate during peak.

Can you confirm which GPU configs you recommend (A100-80GB vs H100 vs L40s) for an SLO-backed Dedicated reservation that meets the above? Also, any guidance on reserved throughput vs autoscale bursting to cover spikes?

If useful, I can share a short set of sample prompts and traffic shape.

—Alex
Senior Platform Eng, Acme Payments
From: rafael_mendes@redwood.ai

Alex — thanks for the clear SLOs, that helps a lot. Recap + recommended next steps below.

Recap of call:
- Target: P95 <= 200ms for single-turn ~120-token prompts; streaming required.
- Concurrency: typical 150 active sessions, spike to 300.
- Throughput estimate: ~10k tokens/sec at peak.
- Security: will use Dedicated with customer VPC peering; encryption + audit logs required (we noted SOC2 evidence).

Preliminary sizing recommendations (high level):
1) GPU family: H100 for best latency at high concurrency when using fp16/llm.int8 quantized variants; A100-80GB is a close alternative for cost-sensitive configs; L40s perform well for cost-optimized inference but have higher tail latency at large concurrency.
2) Node sizing: for your target we recommend starting with a 4-node pool of H100 (reserved) tuned for low-latency with continuous batching disabled for single-turn SLOs, plus an autoscale burst pool (on-demand) of 4 additional H100s for spikes.
3) Reserved throughput: target a reservation sized to cover 85% of observed peak tokens/sec (so ~8.5k tokens/sec) to keep SLOs under reservation; rely on burst pool for the final 15% spike capacity.
4) Streaming: use our streaming-enabled runtime with incremental token flush every 50 tokens; we'll validate end-to-end websocket performance in the POC.

Attachments: I attached a short sizing workbook and a GPU comparison PDF — they include estimated P95 numbers from our benchmark harness and cost trade-offs.

Next steps:
- Please share a 1-hour time block next week for an engineering sync (we'll bring an infra engineer to validate network/peering and a runtime engineer to confirm streaming behavior).
- Share a small representative traffic sample and a couple of typical prompts (redacted) so we can run a targeted perf test.
- I'll open a scoped POC quote and reserve the initial 4-node pool on paper pending approvals.

I'll loop Marissa and Aditya for the POC coordination.

Best,
Rafael
Account Exec — Redwood Inference

Adding some engineering detail from our runtime benchmarks to help with sizing. Numbers are P95 generation latency for a 120-token single-turn prompt; model = redwood-13B-quant (int8); network + app overhead excluded.

- Single H100 (optimized runtime) serving dedicated: P95 ~= 70ms at 40 concurrent streams; throughput ~= 300 tokens/sec per GPU under low batching.
- Single A100-80GB: P95 ~= 95ms at 40 concurrent; throughput ~= 260 tokens/sec.
- Single L40s: P95 ~= 130ms at 40 concurrent; throughput ~= 180 tokens/sec.

Sizing math (rough):
- To hit 10k tokens/sec with H100: ~34 GPUs (10,000 / 300). For concurrency SLOs we recommend overprovisioning to reduce queuing; so 40 reserved H100s for heavy sustained load would be conservative.
- Hybrid approach: reserve 12 H100s (~3.6k tokens/sec) to cover base load and rely on burst pool (on-demand) of 20–30 H100s for peaks; autoscaling policies to prioritize latency-sensitive routes.

Notes: these numbers assume minimal batching to preserve low tail latency for interactive flows. If you can accept slightly higher P95 (e.g., 250–300ms), we can use more aggressive batching and reduce GPU count by ~30%.

Happy to run a targeted perf test if you can share the sample prompts/traffic.

—Marissa
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — very helpful. A few clarifying Qs before we schedule the perf sync: 
1) The 300 tokens/sec per H100 number — does that account for streaming overhead (token flush every 50 tokens) and websocket latencies?
2) For burst handling, what’s the cold-start time for spinning up new nodes in your autoscale pool (and any warm pool recommendations)?
3) Any recommended observability knobs we should enable to correlate user-facing latency with token-level processing?

We'll prepare redacted prompts and a 30-min traffic sample today and share via the Drive link. Also happy to block next Wed for the engineering sync.

—Alex
From: aditya_rao@redwood.ai
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acme.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, rafael_mendes@redwood.ai
Date: Sat, 18 Jul 2026 09:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery — Dedicated capacity & performance

Alex — quick answers: 
1) Our 300 tokens/sec/H100 estimate for single-turn includes streaming flush every 50 tokens measured on our lab harness (adds ~5–8ms flush overhead per 50-token chunk). Real-world websocket RTT will add client-side latency; we recommend testing end-to-end to quantify RTT.
2) Cold-start: provisioning a fresh H100 node (cloud-on-demand) ~6–9 minutes; using warm standby images we’ve reduced effective time to ~45–90 seconds for new containers on already provisioned hosts. For SLOs that must be strict, we recommend a small warm pool (10–15% of expected peak) to keep fast scaling.
3) Observability: enable per-token tracing, request-level trace IDs, and per-route P95/P99 dashboards. We’ll share a Grafana dashboard template as part of the POC.

I’ll also drop the perf harness runbook into the shared Drive folder. Looking forward to the sample prompts.

—Aditya
Sr. Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
